name: himachali chana madra
notes:
Boil the chickpeas in turmeric first. When adding chickpeas to masala with yogurt / raisins / almonds, do not add more water, the recipe is hydrophobic. The almonds also need to be soaked for a few hours before adding. Note that I think ghee makes it worse. Porcini mushroom powder is non-indian but it helps a ton by adding depth, and lemon adds brightness. Cilantro is better than kasoori if available.

FENNEL AND CLOVES ARE KEY SPICES HERE: chana madra leans on warm, sweet, slightly anise-leaning spices more than the cumin/coriander base most other indian curries do. Fennel seeds and whole cloves carry a lot of the dish's signature character — without them it reads as a generic yogurt-chickpea curry rather than the himachali madra it actually is. Bloom both in oil at the tempering stage (along with bay leaf and any other whole spices). Cloves can be assertive, so don't go heavy — a few whole cloves are plenty.

ONION TREATMENT — COULD GO EITHER WAY: unlike chana masala and rajma (see chana-masala and rajma), chana madra doesn't have a clear winner between blended and coarse onions. Both work. Blended boiled onions balance the yogurt nicely (smooth-on-smooth), and that's a real argument for going that direction. But the recipe already has almonds, raisins, and peppers contributing chunky elements — this is more of a stew than a smooth gravy, and coarse onions don't read out of place. Pick whichever fits the texture you want on the day; both are defensible here.

EGGPLANT WORKS HERE — PAIRS WITH THE YOGURT AND PEPPERS: eggplant fits chana madra as another chunky vegetable component. Works with the yogurt and slots in alongside the anaheim + serrano peppers. Cube and pre-cook (sauté in oil until soft and browned, or bake at ~400°F until tender) before folding in — the yogurt-based sauce here doesn't have the covered-steam mechanism that italian-tomato-white-beans uses to cook raw eggplant on top, so pre-cook is the right path. Add with the chickpeas so it warms through and picks up sauce flavor.

=== EXPERIMENTS (WHAT WORKED, WHAT DIDN'T) ===

SUCCESSFUL — DICED EGGPLANT INTO THE BASE: adding diced eggplant to the base worked. See eggplant note above.

FAILED — TOASTED WALNUTS INSTEAD OF SOAKED ALMONDS: swapping toasted walnuts in for soaked almonds pulled the dish dry and unsatisfying. Chana madra already struggles with having enough liquid, and the walnuts made this worse — they absorb sauce rather than contributing it back the way soaked almonds do. Soaked almonds are the right pick; don't sub walnuts.

FAILED — TOO LITTLE YOGURT + SMASHED CHICKPEAS AS SUBSTRATE: tried limiting the amount of yogurt and relying on smashed chickpeas to give the sauce body. Didn't work — with too little yogurt and mashed chickpeas doing the substrate job, the dish turned into a tough-textured hummus. Yogurt is the right substrate; don't compensate for wanting less yogurt by mashing chickpeas.

GREEK YOGURT IS TOUGH BECAUSE IT LACKS LIQUID: this is what tempted the too-little-yogurt experiment above. Greek yogurt is thicker than regular yogurt and doesn't add much moisture to the sauce, which is a problem because chana madra is already hydrophobic and pulled dry easily. The trap: you add greek yogurt, the dish reads thick and tangy, so you're tempted to add more (more tang) or less (more chickpea-mash-substrate). Better fix: use regular (not greek) yogurt if you can, so the yogurt itself supplies the liquid the dish needs.

WANT TO TRY — ROASTED + FOOD-PROCESSED EGGPLANT AS SUBSTRATE: instead of mashing chickpeas to add substrate, try roasting eggplant and running it through a food processor. Eggplant purée could add body and moisture at the same time (unlike mashed chickpeas which are dry), and it stays in the flavor register the recipe is already going for (see eggplant note above). Untested; next time yogurt-thickness feels wrong this is the direction to try before mashing chickpeas.
